content: There is preclinical evidence from studies conducted on various animal species that suggests opioid peptides may play a role in the pathophysiology of different types of shock, including endotoxic, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, spinal, and anaphylactic shock. Naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist, has been proposed as a potential treatment for shock in humans based on numerous case reports. However, conflicting evidence exists, with some reports failing to support its efficacy. This ongoing debate prompted a meta-analysis to evaluate the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of naloxone in treating shock in humans. The primary objective of this analysis was to assess both the effectiveness and safety of naloxone in human shock and to evaluate the methodological quality of the clinical trials conducted on this topic. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, ISI Web of Science, and others, up to December 2008. Additionally, reference lists of included studies were reviewed, and primary investigators of eligible studies were contacted to identify further relevant research. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of naloxone in human shock, regardless of the age of the patients (adults, children, or neonates). Data on study design, interventions, outcomes, and methodological quality were extracted independently by three reviewers. Out of 120 publications reviewed, six clinical trials were selected for inclusion in the meta-analysis. These trials involved a total of 126 patients experiencing various types of shock, including septic, cardiogenic, hemorrhagic, and spinal shock. The reviewers achieved perfect agreement in the selection of studies (100% concordance). The meta-analysis revealed that naloxone therapy was associated with statistically significant improvements in hemodynamic parameters. Specifically, the mean arterial pressure (MAP) was significantly higher in patients treated with naloxone compared to those receiving a placebo. The weighted mean difference in MAP was +9.33 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI]: 7.07 to 11.59 mm Hg), with no evidence of heterogeneity for this outcome. Additionally, the odds ratio for hemodynamic improvement was 0.24 (95% CI: 0.09 to 0.68), indicating a favorable effect of naloxone. Regarding mortality, the death rate was lower in the naloxone-treated group compared to the placebo group, with an odds ratio of 0.59 (95% CI: 0.21 to 1.67). However, this result was not statistically significant and could be attributed to chance. Furthermore, significant heterogeneity was detected for this outcome (P < 0.05), suggesting variability in the results across studies. In conclusion, naloxone appears to improve blood pressure, particularly mean arterial pressure, in patients with shock. However, its clinical utility as a treatment for shock remains uncertain. Additional high-quality randomized controlled trials are necessary to further evaluate the effectiveness and safety of naloxone in this context.
